title: Suppression of orbital ordering and emergence of a glassy magnetic state in a high-entropy spinel vanadate
authors: Shun Ito, Sota Nakakuki, Satoshi Demura, Tadataka Watanabe
abstract: High-entropy oxides provide a unique platform for exploring the interplay between configurational disorder and correlated electronic states. We report on structural, thermodynamic, and magnetic properties of the high-entropy spinel vanadate (Li$_{0.2}$Mg$_{0.2}$Mn$_{0.2}$Co$_{0.2}$Zn$_{0.2}$)V$_2$O$_4$, in which orbital-active V ions occupy the pyrochlore sublattice. X-ray diffraction measurements reveal that the cubic spinel structure is preserved at temperatures down to 5 K without any detectable symmetry lowering. Unlike conventional spinel vanadates exhibiting a symmetry-lowering structural transition driven by orbital ordering, the compound that we study exhibits a suppression of long-range orbital ordering in the high-entropy state. Magnetic susceptibility measurements show glassy magnetic freezing at temperatures below $\sim$20 K, while specific-heat measurements reveal no anomaly associated with long-range ordering down to 3 K. Frequency-dependent ac susceptibility reveals pronounced glassy dynamics. Analyses based on the Mydosh parameter, dynamic scaling law, and Vogel--Fulcher law suggest an intermediate dynamical regime between canonical spin-glass and cluster-glass behavior. Furthermore, Cole--Cole analyses reveal systematic deviations from a single Debye relaxation process, indicating the presence of heterogeneous magnetic relaxation dynamics near the freezing regime. Our results demonstrate that, in a frustrated spinel vanadate, high configurational entropy suppresses long-range orbital ordering and stabilizes a heterogeneous glassy magnetic state, highlighting the combined roles of geometrical frustration, orbital degrees of freedom, and configurational disorder in high-entropy magnets.
summary: This paper uses high-entropy spinel vanadates to study the competition between orbital ordering and disorder. Experimentally, they show that the random cation distribution suppresses long-range structural transitions associated with orbital order. Instead, the system settles into a complex, heterogeneous glassy magnetic state, highlighting the crucial role of quenched disorder in correlated oxides.
main_problem: The study investigates how high configurational disorder influences the interplay between orbital degrees of freedom, geometrical frustration, and magnetic ordering in spinel vanadates.
main_result: High entropy suppresses long-range orbital ordering, preventing structural symmetry lowering, while simultaneously stabilizing a heterogeneous glassy magnetic state characterized by complex relaxation dynamics.
method: The research combines structural characterization using X-ray diffraction with detailed thermodynamic and magnetic measurements (AC/DC susceptibility, specific heat).
model_or_system: The physical system is the high-entropy spinel vanadate $(	ext{Li}_{0.2}	ext{Mg}_{0.2}	ext{Mn}_{0.2}	ext{Co}_{0.2}	ext{Zn}_{0.2})	ext{V}_2	ext{O}_4$, where V ions form a geometrically frustrated pyrochlore sublattice.
key_observables: Structural symmetry (absence of peak splitting), magnetic susceptibility ($\chi'$ and $\chi''$), specific heat anomalies, and relaxation dynamics analyzed via Cole-Cole plots.
important_parameters: Temperature regimes (down to 3 K), disorder concentration (high entropy), and characteristic freezing temperatures ($T_f \sim 17-22$ K).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the observed glassy dynamics are due to a spatially nonuniform spin-orbital state induced by random A-site cation distribution.
figures_summary: Figures show preserved cubic XRD structure down to low temperatures, ZFC/FC magnetic bifurcation below $\sim 17$ K, and AC susceptibility plots demonstrating frequency-dependent relaxation indicative of glassy dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by first establishing the structural stability (XRD) contrasting with orbital ordering expectations. It then measures bulk magnetism (M(T), C(T)) to rule out conventional long-range order, culminating in detailed AC susceptibility analysis using multiple models (Vogel–Fulcher, dynamic scaling) to characterize the glassy state.
why_interesting: The work provides experimental evidence of how quenched structural disorder can fundamentally alter the ground state by suppressing collective orbital ordering, leading to complex, frustrated magnetic dynamics relevant to correlated electron physics.
